title: Chanda Mama Comes to See You
story:
Chanda mama, up so high,
round and white in the big dark sky.

He looks down. He sees the trees.
He looks down. He sees the roof.
He looks down… and he sees YOU.

"Hello, little one," says chanda mama.
"I came all this way to see you."

He brings you silver on the floor.
He brings you silver on the wall.
He brings you silver on your cheek.

Chanda mama, up so high,
round and white in the big dark sky.

Now close your eyes. He is watching.
Now close your eyes. He will stay.
Chanda mama will stay all night,
and go away with the morning light.
repeating_line: Chanda mama, up so high, round and white in the big dark sky.
how_they_join_in: Not yet — and that is expected. This line is your anchor, not theirs. It keeps the telling steady and gives the story a shape the baby begins to recognise. Watch for the participation that is actually available at this age: stilling, widening eyes, a slowed breath, or turning toward your voice when the familiar line comes.
how_to_tell_it:
Say it slowly — much slower than feels natural. This is a lullaby before it is a story.

Hold your baby against your chest so they feel your voice as a vibration as well as hearing it. That vibration is doing as much work as the words.

Lower your voice with each verse. By the last line you should be almost whispering.

On "and he sees YOU" — pause, then say it warmly, right into their face. This is the moment the baby learns the story is about them.

Use the same tune every night, even if you invent it. Same words, same order, same time. A three-month-old is not following the story; they are learning the shape of your voice and that it means sleep is coming.
what_this_builds: Rhythm and prosody recognition. Sleep association. The sound patterns of language before meaning. Bonding through voice and vibration.

title: Yeh Kya Hai? A Body Story
story:
Yeh kya hai? This is your nose.
Little nose, soft nose, choti si naak.

Yeh kya hai? These are your eyes.
Two eyes, bright eyes, looking at me.

Yeh kya hai? This is your mouth.
Open mouth, round mouth, saying "aah".

Yeh kya hai? This is your hand.
Five fingers, small fingers, holding on tight.

Yeh kya hai? This is your tummy.
Round tummy, warm tummy — I'm going to kiss it!

Yeh kya hai? These are your feet.
Two feet, kicking feet, going up and down.

And yeh kya hai?
All of it together —
this is YOU.
And you are mine.
how_they_join_in: Not yet — and that is expected. This line is your anchor, not theirs. It keeps the telling steady and gives the story a shape the baby begins to recognise. Watch for the participation that is actually available at this age: stilling, widening eyes, a slowed breath, or turning toward your voice when the familiar line comes.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a touch story, not a listening story. Touch each part as you name it.

Say "Yeh kya hai?" then pause for three full seconds before answering. That pause is where the conversation lives. You are teaching turn-taking before they can take a turn.

Use it at nappy change and after bath, when they are already undressed and alert. It turns a routine into a language session without adding anything to your day.

Kiss the tummy properly. Make it a real moment — most babies begin to anticipate it within a week, and that anticipation is a genuine cognitive milestone you can watch arrive.

Go slowly. The whole thing should take three minutes, not one.
what_this_builds: Body awareness. Bilingual exposure. Turn-taking through pauses. Anticipation. Touch-language association.
hindi_words: Yeh kya hai (what is this), choti si naak (little nose)

title: The Sounds of Our House
story:
Listen, baby. Our house is talking.

The fan says whirrrr, whirrrr, whirrrr.
Round and round and round.

The cooker says seeeee! One whistle. Two whistles.
Khaana is nearly ready.

The tap says drip. Drip. Drip.
Water falling, one drop at a time.

The door says creeeeak when it opens,
and thud when it closes.

Outside, a crow says kaa! kaa!
He is sitting on the wall.

A scooter goes past. Brrrrmmm.
Away, away, away it goes.

And now — shhh.
Listen.
Do you hear that?

That is my heart. Dhak. Dhak. Dhak.
It is beating for you.
repeating_line: Listen, baby. Our house is talking.
how_they_join_in: Not yet — and that is expected. This line is your anchor, not theirs. It keeps the telling steady and gives the story a shape the baby begins to recognise. Watch for the participation that is actually available at this age: stilling, widening eyes, a slowed breath, or turning toward your voice when the familiar line comes.
how_to_tell_it:
Make every sound properly. Whirr for a long breath. The cooker whistle high and sharp. This is a performance, not a reading.

Best told while carrying them around the house, pointing at each thing as you name it. The fan, then the kitchen, then the door.

Pause after each sound and let the real sound happen if it does. If the actual fan is whirring, stop and let them hear it.

At the end, hold them against your chest for the heartbeat line. Say "dhak, dhak" in time with your actual heartbeat if you can find it.

This story works from birth and keeps working — at eight months they will start pointing at the fan when you begin.
what_this_builds: Auditory discrimination. Sound-object association. Early vocabulary. Attention to environmental sound.

title: Where Is Baby?
story:
Where is baby?
Where has baby gone?

I look under the pillow. Not there.
I look behind the door. Not there.
I look inside my chappal. Not there!

Is baby in the kitchen?
No. Only the dal is in the kitchen.

Is baby on the balcony?
No. Only a crow is on the balcony.

Is baby under this cloth?
Hmm. Let me look…

BOO! There you are!
There is my baby!
I found you!

Let's do it again.
Where is baby?
Where has baby gone?
repeating_line: Where is baby? Where has baby gone?
how_they_join_in: Still entirely yours to say. Their part is physical — a kick, a smile, a whole-body wriggle as the line arrives. By around five months many babies begin to anticipate it, tensing slightly just before it comes. That anticipation is the joining in.
how_to_tell_it:
This is the peek-a-boo story and it is the most important one at this age. Object permanence is forming right now and this is how you feed it.

Put a light muslin over your own face, not the baby's, for the first few weeks. Over their face can feel alarming; over yours is a game.

Build the tension slowly. Look genuinely puzzled. Search under things properly.

On "BOO!" — big face, big smile, big voice. Then immediately soften so it does not startle.

Then say "let's do it again" and do it again. And again. Twenty times is not too many. They cannot say anything back — their participation is the kick, the wriggle, the anticipatory stilling just before you reappear.

Over weeks, extend the hidden time by a second or two. That extension is the developmental work.
what_this_builds: Object permanence. Anticipation. Cause and effect. Emotional regulation through excitement and recovery.

title: Ek Chidiya, Do Chidiya
story:
Ek chidiya — one little bird —
sitting on the mango tree.
Chirp, chirp.

Do chidiya — two little birds —
sitting on the mango tree.
Chirp chirp, chirp chirp.

Teen chidiya — three little birds —
sitting on the mango tree.
Chirp chirp, chirp chirp, chirp chirp!

Then comes the wind. Whoooosh!

And ek chidiya flies away. Bye bye!
And do chidiya fly away. Bye bye!
And teen chidiya fly away. Bye bye bye!

Now the mango tree is quiet.
Only leaves. Only the wind.

But look — here comes ek chidiya, coming back.
Chirp, chirp.
Sitting on the mango tree again.
repeating_line: Ek chidiya, do chidiya, teen chidiya — sitting on the mango tree.
how_they_join_in: Still entirely yours to say. Their part is physical — a kick, a smile, a whole-body wriggle as the line arrives. By around five months many babies begin to anticipate it, tensing slightly just before it comes. That anticipation is the joining in.
how_to_tell_it:
Use your fingers as the birds. One finger, two fingers, three fingers, held up in front of their face.

Chirp with a high squeaky voice, quite different from your speaking voice. Babies orient strongly to pitch changes.

The "whoooosh" is a real breath across their face or hair. They will feel it and it usually produces a startle then a smile.

Flutter your fingers away for the flying, out to the sides and behind your back.

The return at the end matters — this is a story about things coming back, which is exactly the reassurance a baby of this age is working on.

Numbers mean nothing to them yet. You are planting the sound of counting, not the concept.
what_this_builds: Number word exposure. Bilingual counting. Anticipation. Sound-action pairing. Hand tracking.

title: The Little Hands Story
story:
These two hands.
This one and this one.

What can they do?

They can open — like a flower.
Open, open, open.

They can close — like a fist.
Close, close, close.

They can clap. Tali bajao!
Clap, clap, clap.

They can wave. Ta-ta!
Wave, wave, wave.

They can reach — up, up, up, all the way up.

They can hold. Hold my finger.
Ooh, so tight!

And these two hands — this one and this one —
they can come together,
right in the middle,
and touch.

Well done, little hands.
Well done.
repeating_line: These two hands. This one and this one.
how_they_join_in: Still entirely yours to say. Their part is physical — a kick, a smile, a whole-body wriggle as the line arrives. By around five months many babies begin to anticipate it, tensing slightly just before it comes. That anticipation is the joining in.
how_to_tell_it:
Do every movement with their hands, gently, as you say it. You are moving them; they are not moving themselves yet, and that is fine.

Go slowly enough that they can watch their own hands move. At this age they are discovering their hands exist and this story points at that discovery.

The "come together in the middle" is the important one — bringing hands to the midline is a real motor milestone at this age and this story practises it daily.

"Tali bajao" and "ta-ta" are worth keeping in Hindi. They are the phrases the whole extended family will use, and hearing them here first means the child recognises them later.

End with genuine praise. They did not do anything, but the tone teaches that effort is noticed.
what_this_builds: Midline crossing. Hand awareness. Motor imitation groundwork. Bilingual gesture vocabulary.

title: The Cat Who Hid
story:
There was a billi. A small white billi.
And the billi loved to hide.

"Billi, where are you?"

Is she behind the door?
Let me look… no. Not behind the door.

Is she under the bed?
Let me look… no. Not under the bed.

Is she inside the basket?
Let me look… no. Not inside the basket.

Then — listen!
Meow.

Meow?
Meow!

Is she behind the curtain?

Let me look…

MEOW! There she is!
There is the billi!
She was hiding all the time.

Come here, billi. Come here.
Sit with us.
No more hiding now.

…Until tomorrow.
how_they_join_in: Bodily, not verbal. A bounce, an arm wave, a turn toward you, sometimes a bang of the hand. Some babies begin reaching for the object in the story at the repeated line. No words at all yet, and none expected.
how_to_tell_it:
Hide something real — a soft toy, a cloth cat, anything. Actually hide it, and actually look for it. A baby at eight months can follow this.

Say "let me look" and then genuinely look. Lift the cloth, open the basket. Let them see the searching.

The "meow" from behind the curtain should come as a surprise. Make the meow from a different direction if you can — behind your back, to one side. They will turn toward it, which is the sound-localisation work happening.

Let them find it. Hold the cloth so they can pull it off themselves. Pulling the cloth away is the whole developmental point at this age.

Repeat with the same hiding place for several days before changing it. Predictability first, novelty second.
what_this_builds: Object permanence. Sound localisation. Search behaviour. Anticipation. Pulling and grasping.

title: Roti Roti, Round and Round
story:
Take the atta. Put it in the bowl.
Add the paani. Just a little.

Now mix. Mix, mix, mix.
Squish, squish, squish.

Now roll it. Roll a small ball.
Round and round and round.

Now press it. Press it flat.
Press, press, press.

Now the belan. Roll it out.
This way. That way.
This way. That way.
Bigger. Bigger. Bigger!

Now on the tawa. Sssss!
One side. Turn it over.
Other side. Ssssss!

And now — look!
It goes puff!
Big and round like a balloon.

Roti is ready.
Ghee on top.
For whom?

For YOU.
repeating_line: Roll it, press it, roll it out — this way, that way.
how_they_join_in: Bodily, not verbal. A bounce, an arm wave, a turn toward you, sometimes a bang of the hand. Some babies begin reaching for the object in the story at the repeated line. No words at all yet, and none expected.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a doing story. Tell it while you are actually making rotis, with the baby in a bouncer or on a hip nearby.

Every sound is real — the ssss on the tawa, the mixing, the rolling. Let them hear the actual thing.

"Puff" should be big and delighted. That moment when a roti puffs is genuinely dramatic and worth performing.

If you are not cooking, do the actions in the air with their hands. Rolling, pressing, flattening.

The ending — "for YOU" — is where they light up. Point at them. Every time.

This story teaches the vocabulary of an Indian kitchen, which is where a great deal of your child's life will happen.
what_this_builds: Sequence and process. Kitchen vocabulary. Sound-action pairing. Anticipation of a known ending.
hindi_words: atta (flour), paani (water), belan (rolling pin), tawa (griddle), ghee, roti

title: Up and Down, Baby
story:
Up goes the baby. UP!
Down comes the baby. Down.

Up goes the crow. Up to the wall.
Down comes the crow. Down to the ground.

Up goes the ball. Up in the air.
Down comes the ball. Bounce, bounce, bounce.

Up goes the sun. Up in the morning.
Down goes the sun. Down at night.

Up go your arms. Way up high.
Down come your arms. Down in my lap.

Up, up, up.
Down, down, down.

And now — the biggest one.

Ready?
Uuuuuup!

…and down.
Safe. In my arms.
Always safe.
repeating_line: Up, up, up. Down, down, down.
how_they_join_in: Bodily, not verbal. A bounce, an arm wave, a turn toward you, sometimes a bang of the hand. Some babies begin reaching for the object in the story at the repeated line. No words at all yet, and none expected.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a movement story. Lift them on every "up" and lower them on every "down". Gently, and never above your head at this age.

Vary the speed. Sometimes a slow up, sometimes a quick one. The unpredictability is what makes them laugh.

Pause before the last "uuuuup" and let the anticipation build. Say "ready?" and wait. At eight months many babies will start to tense with excitement — that anticipation is a real cognitive achievement and you can watch it appear.

End with them held close and still. The story goes from excitement to calm, which is regulation practice.

The words "up" and "down" are among the earliest spatial concepts and this story teaches both at once, through the body.
what_this_builds: Spatial concepts. Vestibular input. Anticipation. Excitement and recovery. Early opposites.

title: The Hungry Little Elephant
story:
There was a little hathi. A small grey hathi.
And the little hathi was hungry.

He went to the mango tree.
"Are there mangoes for me?"

He looked up with his long, long trunk.
Up, up, up.
But the mangoes were too high.

He tried again. Stretch!
Still too high.

He tried again. Stretch, stretch!
Still too high.

Then came the wind. Whoooosh!

And the mangoes went…
shake, shake, shake…

and one mango fell.
THUMP.

Right in front of the little hathi.

He picked it up with his trunk.
He put it in his mouth.

Mmmmm.

"Thank you, wind," said the little hathi.
And he ate his mango in the shade of the tree.
how_they_join_in: Bodily, not verbal. A bounce, an arm wave, a turn toward you, sometimes a bang of the hand. Some babies begin reaching for the object in the story at the repeated line. No words at all yet, and none expected.
how_to_tell_it:
Use your arm as the trunk — hold it out in front of your nose and swing it. Babies find this genuinely funny.

The three stretches should escalate. First one ordinary, second one more effortful, third one enormous with a groan.

"Whoooosh" is a real breath on their face.

"THUMP" should be sudden and loud enough to surprise slightly, then immediately go soft again.

The "mmmmm" at the end — really do it, with your eyes closed. They copy this expression before they copy any word.

This story has a shape babies begin to recognise at this age: want something, try, fail, try, fail, then succeed. It is their first plot.
what_this_builds: Story structure (problem and resolution). Persistence as a theme. Animal vocabulary. Anticipation across repeated attempts.

title: The Crow and the Pot
story:
It was a hot day. Very, very hot.

A kauwa was flying. Kaa! Kaa!
And the kauwa was thirsty.
So thirsty.

He looked for water. No water here.
He looked for water. No water there.

Then he saw a pot.
A big clay pot — a matka.

He flew down. He looked inside.
There WAS water!
But the water was far, far down at the bottom.

He put his beak in. Too far.
He stretched. Too far.
He could not reach.

The kauwa thought.
And thought.
And thought.

Then he saw a stone.

Plop. He dropped it in.
Plop. Another one.
Plop, plop, plop.

And the water came up…
up…
UP.

And the clever kauwa drank his water.
Glug, glug, glug.

Clever, clever kauwa.
how_they_join_in: A gesture, or occasionally a rough single sound. Most babies do the action long before the word — waving, pointing, or reaching on cue. If an approximation of one syllable appears, that is ahead of schedule rather than typical.
how_to_tell_it:
The "plop" is the part they will join in on. Say it clearly and pause before each one so they can anticipate.

Use a real cup and small objects if you can — drop something in and let them watch the level change. At eleven months this is fascinating and it makes the story concrete.

"He thought, and thought, and thought" — put your finger on your chin and go silent for three seconds. The pause is the drama.

The rising water should rise in your voice too. Up… up… UP, getting higher each time.

This is the first Panchatantra story most Indian children hear and it works from about ten months as a sound-and-action story, long before they understand the cleverness. They will understand that part at three.
what_this_builds: Problem-solving as a story shape. Cause and effect. Repetition with anticipation. First exposure to a classic tale.

title: Nahaane Ka Time — Bath Time
story:
Nahaane ka time!
Bath time, bath time!

First the clothes come off.
Off with the shirt — over your head. Peek!
Off with the pants — one leg, two legs.

Now, into the water.
Chhap! Chhap!
Splash, splash, splash.

Wash the hands. Wash, wash.
Wash the feet. Wash, wash.
Wash the tummy — ooh, that tickles!
Wash the back. Wash, wash.

Now the head. Careful, careful.
Close your eyes. Tip back.
Paani coming… and done!

Now the mug. Fill it up.
Poooour. All the way down.

One more. Poooour.

All clean!

Now the towel. Big and soft.
Wrap you up like a roti.
Rub, rub, rub.

Warm and dry and clean.
Ready for a kiss.
repeating_line: Nahaane ka time! Bath time, bath time!
how_they_join_in: A gesture, or occasionally a rough single sound. Most babies do the action long before the word — waving, pointing, or reaching on cue. If an approximation of one syllable appears, that is ahead of schedule rather than typical.
how_to_tell_it:
Tell it during the actual bath, every day, in the same order. The story becomes the routine and the routine becomes predictable, which is what makes bath time easy.

"Peek!" when the shirt comes over their head — a mini peek-a-boo built into undressing.

Slow right down for the head-washing part. Many babies dislike this and a calm, slow, narrated approach helps considerably.

"Wrap you up like a roti" — actually roll them in the towel. This is the bit they will ask for later.

By twelve months many babies begin doing the actions before you say them. When that happens, pause and let them lead.
what_this_builds: Routine sequencing. Body vocabulary. Predictability and cooperation. Bilingual everyday phrases.
hindi_words: nahaane ka time (bath time), chhap (splash), paani (water), roti

title: Who Says What?
story:
The gaay says moooo.
Moo, moo.

The bakri says mehhh.
Meh, meh.

The kutta says bhow bhow!
Bhow! Bhow!

The billi says meow.
Meow, meow.

The kauwa says kaa!
Kaa! Kaa!

The murga says kukdoo-koo!
In the morning. Very loud!

The hathi says…
(big breath)
PAAAAAOOO!

And the little baby says…

what does the little baby say?

Hmm?

The little baby says…
"Ma-ma-ma-ma!"

And that is my favourite sound of all.
how_they_join_in: A gesture, or occasionally a rough single sound. Most babies do the action long before the word — waving, pointing, or reaching on cue. If an approximation of one syllable appears, that is ahead of schedule rather than typical.
how_to_tell_it:
Pause before every animal sound. Most babies at this age will not make the sound yet — but many will look at you expectantly, or bounce, or open their mouth. That anticipation is the participation. If a rough approximation comes, treat it as a triumph.

Use different voices — the goat high and wobbly, the elephant enormous, the crow harsh.

The elephant needs a real deep breath before it. Build the anticipation.

At the end, pause properly on "what does the little baby say?" and wait five full seconds. Whatever sound they make, treat it as the answer and be delighted.

Use the Hindi animal names as the main ones. Your child will hear gaay and kutta far more often in daily life than cow and dog, and this is the age to attach the sound to the word.
what_this_builds: Animal vocabulary in Hindi. Sound imitation. Turn-taking. Early word production. Anticipation.
hindi_words: gaay (cow), bakri (goat), kutta (dog), billi (cat), kauwa (crow), murga (rooster), hathi (elephant)

title: Chalo, Let's Go Outside
story:
Chalo! Let's go outside.

First — chappal. One foot. Two feet.
Ready?

Open the door. Creeeeak.

Down the steps. One, two, three.
Careful, careful.

Now — look up.
The sky is so big.
Blue and big and far away.

Look at the tree.
The leaves go shhh-shhh in the wind.

Touch the tree. Rough! Bumpy!

Look — a crow on the wall.
Kaa! Kaa!
He is looking at us.

Look — a scooter. Brrrmm!
It goes away, away, away.

Feel the dhoop on your face.
Warm. Very warm.

Now feel the shade.
Cool. Ahhh.

Warm… cool.
Warm… cool.

Okay. Time to go home.
Say bye-bye to the tree.
Bye-bye!

Say bye-bye to the crow.
Bye-bye!

Chalo. Andar chalein.
Let's go in.
how_they_join_in: A gesture, or occasionally a rough single sound. Most babies do the action long before the word — waving, pointing, or reaching on cue. If an approximation of one syllable appears, that is ahead of schedule rather than typical.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a walking story, told outdoors while it happens. Do not tell it sitting down.

Stop at each thing and let them actually look, actually touch. The tree bark, the warm patch of sun, the shade. Twenty seconds each.

"Warm… cool… warm… cool" — step in and out of the shade as you say it. This temperature contrast is genuinely interesting to a baby.

Wave properly at the end. Waving bye-bye is a milestone gesture at this age and this story practises it twice, in a real context.

Same route, same things, every day. By twelve months they will point at the tree before you get there.
what_this_builds: Sensory vocabulary. Outdoor exploration. Gesture practice (waving). Temperature contrast. Bilingual transitions.
hindi_words: chalo (let's go), chappal (slippers), dhoop (sunshine), andar chalein (let's go inside)

title: The Monkey Who Took the Caps
story:
A topiwala walked down the road.
He had a big pile of caps on his head.
Topi, topi, topi — all the way up.

"Topi le lo! Caps for sale!" he called.

He walked and walked. He got tired.
So he sat under a big tree and closed his eyes.
And he fell asleep. Zzzzzz.

While he slept — the bandars came.
One monkey. Two monkeys. Many monkeys!

Chi chi chi! Down they came.
And each monkey took a topi.
And each monkey put it on his head.
And up, up, up they went, back into the tree.

The topiwala woke up.
He touched his head. Only ONE topi left!

He looked up.
Bandars! Everywhere! All wearing his caps!

"Give them back!" he shouted.
"Chi chi chi!" said the monkeys.

He waved his hands.
The monkeys waved their hands.

He stamped his feet.
The monkeys stamped their feet.

He scratched his head.
The monkeys scratched their heads.

Then the topiwala had an idea.

He took off his own topi — and threw it on the ground.

And all the monkeys took off their topis —
and threw them on the ground!

The topiwala picked them all up.
"Thank you, bandars!" he laughed.
And off he went down the road.

"Topi le lo! Caps for sale!"
how_they_join_in: The action, not the words. Clapping, stamping, reaching, shaking the head. Most children here have fewer than ten words, so do not expect the line itself. A vowel sound roughly in the right place is a very good outcome.
how_to_tell_it:
This is the best action story of the toddler years. Every copying moment is a moment for your child to copy too.

Do each action and let them copy: wave, stamp, scratch. Pause after each so they can join.

"Chi chi chi" is yours to say at this age — most children here have very few words. What they will join in with is the action: the waving, stamping and scratching. Pause on each one and let them copy the movement. The words come months later.

The throwing of the cap at the end — mime it big, and have something to actually throw if you can. A cloth, a dupatta.

Voices: the topiwala tired and grumpy, the monkeys high and fast.

This story teaches imitation as a plot device, which is exactly what a fourteen-month-old is doing all day anyway.
what_this_builds: Imitation. Action words. Cause and effect. Problem-solving. Joining in with a refrain.
hindi_words: topiwala (cap seller), topi (cap), bandar (monkey), topi le lo (buy caps)

title: Where Did the Ball Go?
story:
A red ball. A round red ball.

Bounce, bounce, bounce.

Bounce it here. Bounce it there.
Bounce it high — up in the air!

And then…

the ball rolled away.

Roll, roll, roll.

Where did the ball go?
Under the sofa? Let's look.
No ball there.

Behind the door? Let's look.
No ball there.

In the bucket? Let's look.
No ball there!

Then — a little sound.
Thud.

What was that?

Under the bed!
There it is!
The red ball, under the bed.

Reach in. Stretch. Stretch!

Got it!

The red ball is back.
Bounce, bounce, bounce.

Hooray!
how_they_join_in: The action, not the words. Clapping, stamping, reaching, shaking the head. Most children here have fewer than ten words, so do not expect the line itself. A vowel sound roughly in the right place is a very good outcome.
how_to_tell_it:
Use a real ball. Actually roll it away. Actually search.

Let them do the searching. At fourteen months a child can genuinely look under a sofa, and this story turns that into a game with a shape.

"Let's look" — pause and let them move first.

The stretching should be effortful and comic. Groan a bit.

The "hooray" at the end with arms up. Most children start doing the arms before the word.

Vary where you hide it as they get better at this. That variation is what keeps the search skill developing.
what_this_builds: Search behaviour. Spatial words (under, behind, in). Persistence. Object permanence extended.

title: Good Morning, Everyone
story:
The sun comes up.
Good morning, sun!

The crow wakes up. Kaa!
Good morning, crow!

The milkman comes. Ting ting!
Good morning, doodhwala!

Dadi wakes up. She puts on the kettle.
Good morning, Dadi!

Papa wakes up. He looks for his chappals.
Good morning, Papa!

Mumma wakes up. She opens the window.
Good morning, Mumma!

And who is this?
Who is still in bed?
Who has sleepy eyes and messy hair?

It's YOU!

Good morning, my baby!
Good morning, good morning, good morning!

Now — up we get.
The day is waiting.
how_they_join_in: The action, not the words. Clapping, stamping, reaching, shaking the head. Most children here have fewer than ten words, so do not expect the line itself. A vowel sound roughly in the right place is a very good outcome.
how_to_tell_it:
Tell this in the actual morning, in bed, before getting up. It becomes the wake-up ritual.

Say "good morning" the same way every time — same tune, same warmth. It becomes the sound of the day starting.

Swap in the real people in your house. Nana, Nani, Bua, the actual names. The story should be about their household, not a generic one.

Pause on "who is this?" and let them realise it is them. From fourteen months many children point at themselves here, which is early self-recognition.

Keep it short. Mornings are not the time for a long story.
what_this_builds: Family vocabulary. Daily routine. Self-recognition. Greeting rituals. Sequencing.

title: The Very Muddy Puppy
story:
There was a little kutta. A clean white kutta.

He went outside.

He saw a puddle.
A big brown puddle.

Should he? Should he not?

He SHOULD!

Splash! In he went.
Splash, splash, splash!

Now his paws were brown.
Now his legs were brown.
Now his tummy was brown.
Now his nose was brown!

He rolled. Roll, roll, roll.
Now ALL of him was brown.

"Bhow!" said the muddy kutta. He was very happy.

Then he went home.

His Mumma looked at him.
She looked at his brown paws.
She looked at his brown nose.

"Oh dear," she said. "Nahaane ka time."

Into the water. Chhap!
Scrub, scrub, scrub.
Rub, rub, rub.

Brown water going down, down, down.

And out came…
a clean white kutta again!

"Bhow," he said.

And tomorrow?
Tomorrow he will find that puddle again.
how_they_join_in: The action, not the words. Clapping, stamping, reaching, shaking the head. Most children here have fewer than ten words, so do not expect the line itself. A vowel sound roughly in the right place is a very good outcome.
how_to_tell_it:
The "should he? should he not?" is a real question — pause and let them answer with a sound or a nod.

"He SHOULD!" is loud and delighted. This is a story that is on the child's side about mess, which they appreciate more than adults expect.

Do the scrubbing on them during the washing part. Scrub their arms, their nose.

The last line — "tomorrow he will find that puddle again" — is the joke, and by sixteen months they get it.

This story is useful before or after an actual bath, and it makes mud less of a battle because the story has already permitted it.
what_this_builds: Colour and change. Sequence. Cause and consequence without punishment. Bath vocabulary. Humour.
hindi_words: kutta (dog), bhow (woof), nahaane ka time (bath time), chhap (splash)

title: Ek, Do, Teen — Counting Story
story:
Ek. One mango on the tree.
Just one. Hanging there.

Do. Two crows on the wall.
Kaa! Kaa!

Teen. Three chappals by the door.
One, two, three — wait!
Three?

Somebody has lost a chappal!

Char. Four rotis on the plate.
Hot and round.

Paanch. Five fingers on your hand.
One, two, three, four, five.

Count them again.
Ek, do, teen, char, paanch.

Five fingers.
And on this hand?
Five more!

So many fingers.
So much counting.

Now — one more thing to count.

How many babies are in this room?

Ek.

Just one.
And that one is the best one.
how_they_join_in: The action, not the words. Clapping, stamping, reaching, shaking the head. Most children here have fewer than ten words, so do not expect the line itself. A vowel sound roughly in the right place is a very good outcome.
how_to_tell_it:
Count on their fingers, touching each one. Physical counting, not spoken counting.

The chappal joke — "three? somebody has lost a chappal!" — pause and look around in mock confusion. Toddlers find this genuinely funny.

Say the numbers in Hindi first, then English, consistently in that order. They will not count along yet — at this age they are absorbing the sound and rhythm of a number sequence, which comes long before the concept.

Go slowly. One number per breath.

Point at them for the last line. Every time. That is the payoff and it is why they ask for it again.
what_this_builds: Number word sequence. One-to-one correspondence. Bilingual counting. Finger awareness.
hindi_words: ek, do, teen, char, paanch (one to five), chappal, roti

title: The Thirsty Crow
story:
One hot day, a kauwa was flying.
It was so hot. The sun was burning.
And the kauwa was thirsty. Very thirsty.

"I need paani," said the kauwa. "Where is paani?"

He flew over the field. No water.
He flew over the road. No water.
He flew over the houses. No water.

His wings were tired. His throat was dry.

Then he saw — a matka!
A big clay pot in a garden.

He flew down. Flap, flap, flap.
He looked inside.

Water! There was water!

But the water was low.
Right down at the bottom.

He put his beak in. Not enough.
He stretched his neck. Not enough.
He tipped the pot. It would not move.

"Oh no," said the kauwa.

He sat down and thought.

He looked around.
He saw one stone.
He saw another stone.
Stones everywhere.

And then — the kauwa had an idea!

He picked up a stone. Plop!
Into the water.

He picked up another. Plop!
And another. Plop, plop!

Plop. Plop. Plop.

And the water came up.
Higher.
And higher.
And HIGHER.

Until — the kauwa could reach!

Glug, glug, glug.
He drank and drank.

"Ah," said the clever kauwa. "That's better."

And off he flew, into the blue sky.
how_they_join_in: One word, roughly said — often 'no', 'more', or an animal sound. Expect an approximation rather than the full line, and expect it inconsistently. The action is still doing most of the work.
how_to_tell_it:
They join in on every plop. Pause before each one.

Demonstrate with a real glass and small stones or spoons if you can. The water genuinely rising is the moment the story becomes real for a toddler.

"And then — the kauwa had an idea!" — this is the peak. Big pause, then say it brightly with a finger in the air.

Voices: the crow croaky and tired at the start, brighter at the end.

By eighteen months, ask "what should the crow do?" before revealing the answer. Some will point at the stones.
what_this_builds: Problem-solving. Persistence. Sequence and consequence. Classic tale exposure. Anticipating a solution.

title: No, No, No!
story:
There was a little girl called Meera.
And Meera's favourite word was NO.

"Meera, shall we wear shoes?"
"NO!"

"Meera, shall we eat khaana?"
"NO!"

"Meera, shall we have a bath?"
"NO!"

"Meera, shall we go to the park?"
"NO!… wait."

Hmm.

"Park?"

"HAAN!" said Meera. "Yes! Park!"

So Meera put on her shoes — all by herself.
And Meera ate her khaana — all by herself.

And off they went to the park.

Meera went on the slide. Whoosh!
Meera went on the swing. Up and down!
Meera ran and ran and ran.

Then it was time to go home.

"Meera, shall we go home?"

"NO!"

But it was time.
So home they went.

And at home, Meera had a bath.
And in the bath she said…

"Ha! Bubbles!"

Not "no" this time.

Goodnight, Meera.
how_they_join_in: One word, roughly said — often 'no', 'more', or an animal sound. Expect an approximation rather than the full line, and expect it inconsistently. The action is still doing most of the work.
how_to_tell_it:
They will say NO with you. That is the whole point — this story lets a child use their favourite word in a place where it is welcome, which slightly reduces its power elsewhere.

Say each "NO" differently — one huge, one small, one grumpy.

The "NO!… wait" is the funny bit. Pause properly.

Change the name to your child's name. It works considerably better.

This story is worth telling during the "no" phase because it shows a child who says no and is still loved, and who changes her mind on her own. Do not moralise about it. Just tell it.
what_this_builds: Yes/no concepts. Emotional vocabulary. Self-recognition through a character. Humour about their own behaviour.

title: The Lost Chappal
story:
One chappal by the door.
Only one.

Where is the other one?

Look under the bed.
Not there. Only dust.

Look behind the almirah.
Not there. Only a spider.

Look in the bathroom.
Not there. Only water.

Look in the kitchen.
Not there. Only Dadi making chai.

"Dadi, have you seen my chappal?"
"No, beta. Look outside."

Outside!

Look near the tulsi plant.
Not there.

Look near the gate.
Not there.

Then — what is that?

Under the gate.
Something blue.

It IS the chappal!

But wait — who is that?
A little kutta.
And he is CHEWING it!

"Hey! That's mine!"

The kutta drops it and runs. Bhow bhow!

Pick it up. It is a bit wet.
But it is fine.

One chappal. Two chappals.

Now we can go.

Chalo!
how_they_join_in: One word, roughly said — often 'no', 'more', or an animal sound. Expect an approximation rather than the full line, and expect it inconsistently. The action is still doing most of the work.
how_to_tell_it:
Pause before "not there" — some children at this age will shake their head or make a sound. A head shake is a real answer and worth treating as one. The words themselves usually arrive closer to two.

Look in the real places as you say them. Under the actual bed, behind the actual almirah. This turns the story into a hunt.

Build tension before "something blue" — slow down, drop your voice.

The dog is the funny surprise. Make him fast and cheeky.

At eighteen months this story has a proper shape: a problem, a search, a setback, a resolution. That is their first real plot and it works because the object is one they know.
what_this_builds: Search and sequence. Spatial prepositions. Household vocabulary. Narrative structure with a twist.
hindi_words: chappal (slipper), almirah (cupboard), Dadi, chai, beta (child), tulsi (holy basil), kutta, chalo

title: Baarish! The Rain Story
story:
Look at the sky.
It is grey. All grey.

The wind comes. Whoooosh!
The leaves go shhhh.

Something is coming.

Drip.

One drop.

Drip. Drop.

Two drops.

Drip drop drip drop drip drop —

BAARISH!

Rain, rain, everywhere!

On the roof — tip tip tip.
On the leaves — pat pat pat.
On the road — chhap chhap chhap.
On the window — tap tap tap.

The peacock is dancing!
The frogs are singing! Tarr! Tarr!
The mitti smells so good.

Put out your hand.
Feel it.
Cold! Wet!

Splash in the puddle!
Chhap! Chhap!

And then…

slowly…

the rain gets small again.

Drip drop.

Drip.

And stops.

Now look up.
The sun is coming back.
And there — do you see?

A rainbow.

All the colours in the sky.
how_they_join_in: One word, roughly said — often 'no', 'more', or an animal sound. Expect an approximation rather than the full line, and expect it inconsistently. The action is still doing most of the work.
how_to_tell_it:
Build the rain slowly. One drop, two drops, then the burst. The build is the pleasure.

Tap the different rain sounds on different surfaces — the table, your hand, their tummy. Each surface a different sound.

If it is actually raining, tell it at the window and stop to listen.

"Put out your hand" — if you can, actually do it. Rain on the hand is a memorable sensory moment for a toddler.

Slow right down at the end. The story goes loud to quiet, which makes it usable before a nap.
what_this_builds: Sound words. Weather vocabulary. Building and receding intensity. Sensory language. Colour introduction.
hindi_words: baarish (rain), chhap (splash), mitti (earth/soil), tip tip (rain sound)

title: Sona and the Sleepy Elephant
story:
It was night.
Everyone was going to sleep.

The chidiya went to sleep in the tree.
Chirp… chirp… shh.

The kutta went to sleep by the gate.
Bhow… bhow… shh.

The billi went to sleep on the wall.
Meow… meow… shh.

But the little hathi would NOT go to sleep.

"I am not sleepy," said the hathi.
"I want to play!"

So he walked. Thump, thump, thump.
He splashed in the river. Chhap!
He ate one banana. Two bananas. Three.

Then his legs got heavy.
Thump… thump… thump…

He sat down under the big tree.

His eyes got heavy.
His ears got heavy.
His trunk went down… down… down…

"Maybe," said the hathi, "I am a little bit sleepy."

And he closed his eyes.

Goodnight, chidiya.
Goodnight, kutta.
Goodnight, billi.
Goodnight, little hathi.

And goodnight, YOU.
how_they_join_in: One word, roughly said — often 'no', 'more', or an animal sound. Expect an approximation rather than the full line, and expect it inconsistently. The action is still doing most of the work.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a bedtime story and it should be told in the dark, or nearly.

Start at normal volume and get quieter with every animal. By the elephant's sleepiness you should be whispering.

Slow the "thump, thump, thump" right down as he gets tired. The pacing does the work.

Yawn during the story. Genuinely. Yawning is contagious and it helps.

End with their name if you like — "and goodnight, Aarav." Same words, same order, every night.
what_this_builds: Bedtime routine. Animal vocabulary. Winding down through pacing. Sequence and repetition.

title: The Lion and the Little Mouse
story:
In the jungle there was a big sher.
A very big sher. With a big loud roar.

ROAARRR!

One day the sher was sleeping under a tree.

A little chuha came running.
Squeak, squeak.

He did not see the sher.
He ran right over the sher's paw!

The sher woke up.
He put his big paw on the little chuha.

"Who woke me up?" he roared.

"Please," squeaked the chuha. "Please let me go.
I am so small. One day I will help you."

The sher laughed. "You? Help ME? You are tiny!"

But he laughed so much that he lifted his paw.
And the chuha ran away. Fast, fast, fast.

Some days later —

the sher was walking in the jungle.
And he did not see the net.

A big net! It caught him!

He pulled. He could not get out.
He pushed. He could not get out.

He roared. ROAARRR!

The little chuha heard him.
And he came running.

"I said I would help you," said the chuha.

And with his small sharp teeth —
he began to chew.

Chew, chew, chew.
Chew, chew, chew.

The rope broke!
And the sher was free.

"Thank you, little friend," said the sher.
"Even a small one can help a big one."

And they walked away together.
how_they_join_in: Usually the last word of the line, if you pause and genuinely wait. Two seconds is not long enough — count to five. Many children fill the gap by this point, some still only with a gesture.
how_to_tell_it:
Two very different voices. The lion enormous and slow; the mouse tiny and fast. Toddlers love this contrast and it is what holds their attention through a longer story.

The roar should be big enough to be exciting and not big enough to frighten. Watch their face.

"Chew, chew, chew" is theirs. Pause and let them do it.

Make the net moment tense — the pulling and pushing, the frustration.

At twenty months they will not understand the moral. They will understand that the small one helped the big one, which is enough and is the whole point anyway.
what_this_builds: Longer narrative. Character contrast. Cause and effect across time. Kindness and reciprocity as story shape.

title: Whose Baby Is This?
story:
A little baby was crying in the field.
Someone had lost their baby!

Whose baby is this?

The gaay came. "Moo. Is that my baby?"
She looked. "No. My baby is a calf. My baby says moo."

The bakri came. "Meh. Is that my baby?"
She looked. "No. My baby is a kid. My baby says meh."

The murgi came. "Kuk kuk. Is that my baby?"
She looked. "No. My baby is a chick. My baby says cheep."

The billi came. "Meow. Is that my baby?"
She looked. "No. My baby is a kitten. My baby says mew."

Then — someone came running.
Running fast across the field.

"MY BABY!"

It was the baby's Mumma!

She picked the baby up.
She held the baby tight.

"I was looking everywhere for you," she said.

And the baby stopped crying.
And the baby smiled.

Because when you are lost —
your Mumma always, always comes.
how_they_join_in: Usually the last word of the line, if you pause and genuinely wait. Two seconds is not long enough — count to five. Many children fill the gap by this point, some still only with a gesture.
how_to_tell_it:
The animals should each have their own voice and their own walk if you are standing up.

"Whose baby is this?" is theirs to say with you. It repeats enough that they learn it.

Slow down and make the mother's arrival warm and big. This is a story about being found and it lands emotionally at this age, when separation is on their mind.

End with a hug. Genuinely. The story asks for it.

Useful before or after a daycare start or any separation.
what_this_builds: Animal families. Reassurance about separation. Repetitive question structure. Animal sounds.

title: The Big Big Turnip
story:
Dada planted a seed.
A little seed in the mitti.

He gave it paani. He gave it dhoop.

And it grew.
And it GREW.
And it GREEEEW.

Into a big, big mooli.
The biggest mooli anyone had ever seen.

"Time to pull it out," said Dada.

He held the mooli.
He pulled.

Heave! Ho!

It did not move.

So he called Dadi.

Dadi held Dada. Dada held the mooli.
They pulled.

Heave! Ho!

It did not move.

So they called Mumma.

Mumma held Dadi. Dadi held Dada. Dada held the mooli.
They pulled.

Heave! Ho!

It did not move.

So they called Papa.
And Papa held Mumma, and Mumma held Dadi,
and Dadi held Dada, and Dada held the mooli.

Heave! Ho!

It did NOT move.

Then — a little voice.

"I can help."

It was the baby.

Everybody laughed. "You are too small!"

But the baby held Papa.
And everybody pulled.

Heave!

HO!

And OUT came the mooli!

Everybody fell down. Dhaddam!

And they all laughed and laughed.

And that night, they ate mooli ki sabzi.
And it was delicious.
how_they_join_in: Usually the last word of the line, if you pause and genuinely wait. Two seconds is not long enough — count to five. Many children fill the gap by this point, some still only with a gesture.
how_to_tell_it:
"Heave! Ho!" is the whole story for a toddler. Do it with your whole body — lean back, pull, grunt.

Let them pull with you. Hold their hands and lean back together on each heave.

Each round should get more effortful and funnier.

"Dhaddam!" — fall over. Actually fall over if you can, or fall backwards on the bed with them.

Change the family members to your actual family. Nana, Nani, Bua, Chachu.

The child being the one who makes the difference is the emotional core. Say "it was the baby" while looking right at them.
what_this_builds: Cumulative structure. Family vocabulary. Cooperation. Physical participation. Building anticipation.
hindi_words: Dada, Dadi (grandparents), mitti (soil), paani (water), dhoop (sun), mooli (radish), sabzi (vegetable dish), dhaddam (crash)

title: Too Many Bananas
story:
A bandar found one banana.
"Yum!" he said.

Then he found another.
Two bananas!

Then another. Three!
Then another. Four!
Then another. Five!

Five bananas.

He put one under his arm.
He put one under the other arm.
He put one in his hand.
He put one in his other hand.
And one in his mouth!

He could not walk.
He could not see.
He could not say anything —
his mouth was full!

"Mmmff!" said the bandar.

He tried to move.
Wobble. Wobble.

The banana under his arm fell. Plop!
The banana in his hand fell. Plop!
Another one. Plop!
Another one. Plop!

Only one banana left. In his mouth.

The bandar sat down.
He looked at the bananas on the ground.

Then he ate the one in his mouth.
Chomp, chomp. Mmmm.

Then he picked up one more.
Just one.
And ate it slowly.

And then another.
One at a time.

"That is better," said the bandar.

One at a time is best.
how_they_join_in: Usually the last word of the line, if you pause and genuinely wait. Two seconds is not long enough — count to five. Many children fill the gap by this point, some still only with a gesture.
how_to_tell_it:
The stuffing of the bananas should be physical comedy. Put things under your arms, in your hands, in your mouth. Speak with your mouth full for "mmmff".

Wobble properly. Toddlers laugh at physical instability.

"Plop!" each time, and let them join.

The ending is quiet after the chaos, which is a good shape for a story before a meal or before quiet time.

This story is quietly about not grabbing everything at once, but do not point that out. It lands on its own.
what_this_builds: Counting to five. Humour and physical comedy. Cause and effect. Self-regulation as a theme without moralising.

title: Chotu Goes to the Doctor
story:
Chotu had to go to the doctor.

He did not want to go.
"No doctor," said Chotu.

But Mumma said, "The doctor will just look at you.
And I will hold your hand the whole time."

So they went.

At the clinic there were other children.
One was crying. One was playing with blocks.
Chotu sat on Mumma's lap.

Then it was Chotu's turn.

The doctor said, "Hello, Chotu."

She had a stethoscope. A cold round thing.
"This listens to your heart," she said.
"Shall I listen to Teddy first?"

She put it on Teddy.
Then she put it on Chotu.

Cold! But not scary.

She looked in his ears. One. Two.
She looked in his mouth. "Say aaah."
"Aaah," said Chotu.

Then — one small injection.
Poke!

It hurt a little bit. Chotu cried.
Mumma held him tight.
"That was brave," she said. "It's finished now."

The doctor gave him a sticker.

And on the way home Chotu said —
"Doctor listened to Teddy."

"Yes," said Mumma. "She did."

And Chotu was fine.
He was absolutely fine.
repeating_line: I will hold your hand the whole time.
how_they_join_in: Usually the last word of the line, if you pause and genuinely wait. Two seconds is not long enough — count to five. Many children fill the gap by this point, some still only with a gesture.
how_to_tell_it:
Tell this before a doctor's visit, not after. Two or three times in the days before.

Do the actions on their teddy first, exactly as in the story. This is genuine preparation and it measurably reduces distress.

Do not skip the injection or pretend it does not hurt. "It hurt a little bit" and "that was brave" is honest and builds trust. A child told it will not hurt and then finds it does trusts you less next time.

Keep the tone matter-of-fact throughout. Your calm is the message.

Change Chotu to your child's name.
what_this_builds: Preparation for a real event. Emotional regulation. Honest framing of discomfort. Trust in a caregiver.

title: The Cheeku Who Would Not Share
story:
Cheeku the squirrel had a big pile of nuts.
A BIG pile.

His friend came. "Can I have one nut?"

"No," said Cheeku. "They are all mine."

His friend went away.

Another friend came. "Can I have one nut?"

"No," said Cheeku. "All mine."

That friend went away too.

Cheeku sat with his nuts.
He ate one. Crunch.
He ate another. Crunch.

But it was quiet.
Very quiet.

There was nobody to play with.

Cheeku looked at his big pile of nuts.
Then he looked at the empty tree.

He picked up two nuts.
And he went to find his friends.

"I brought you these," he said.

His friends came back.
They sat together.
They ate nuts. Crunch, crunch, crunch.

And then they played.
Up the tree! Down the tree!
Round and round the tree!

And Cheeku thought —
sharing is not so bad.

It is better with friends.
how_they_join_in: Usually the last word of the line, if you pause and genuinely wait. Two seconds is not long enough — count to five. Many children fill the gap by this point, some still only with a gesture.
how_to_tell_it:
Do not moralise at the end. Just tell it. The story does its own work over many tellings.

"Crunch" is theirs to join in on.

Make the quiet part genuinely quiet. Stop talking for two seconds after "very quiet". That silence is the emotional turn.

Useful during the phase when everything is "mine", which starts around now. Do not tell it immediately after a snatching incident — that turns it into a lecture. Tell it at a calm time.

At twenty months they will not share because of this story. But the idea is being planted.
what_this_builds: Social concepts. Consequence and change of mind. Friendship. Emotional cause and effect.
hindi_words: Cheeku (common pet name; also means sapodilla fruit)

title: The Elephant and the Ants
story:
There was a hathi. A big, proud hathi.

He walked through the jungle.
Thump. Thump. Thump.

And he did not look where he was going.

He knocked down a bird's nest. Crash!
"Sorry?" said the birds.
"I don't care," said the hathi. "I am big."

He splashed all the water out of the pond. Chhap!
"Hey!" said the frogs.
"I don't care," said the hathi. "I am BIG."

Then he walked over a hill of ants.
A whole city of little cheentis.

Thump.

"Our home!" cried the ants.

"I don't care," said the hathi. "You are tiny.
I am the biggest. Nobody can stop me."

And he lay down under a tree to sleep.

The ants looked at each other.

And then — very quietly —
they marched.

One ant. Two ants. Hundreds of ants.

Up the hathi's foot.
Up his leg.
Up his big grey back.

And into his ear.

Tickle. Tickle. TICKLE!

"AAAH!" shouted the hathi.
He jumped up. He shook his head.
He ran to the river. He splashed.

"Stop! Please stop!"

The ants came out.
"Will you look where you are going?" they asked.

"Yes!" said the hathi. "Yes, yes, yes!"

And after that —
the hathi walked carefully.
And he said sorry.
And even the biggest one learned:
small does not mean nothing.
repeating_line: I don't care. I am big.
how_they_join_in: Most of a short repeating line, said along with you. Pausing just before it is what prompts them. They may also start requesting the story by its refrain rather than its title.
how_to_tell_it:
The hathi's voice should be big and boastful. The ants tiny and many — try saying their lines fast and high.

"Thump. Thump. Thump." — stamp your feet.

The tickling is where they laugh. Tickle them during it. That is the payoff.

Slow the ending right down. The change in the elephant should feel like a real change.

At two, they follow this whole story. It is one of the first proper narratives with a character who changes, and that is a real cognitive step.
what_this_builds: Extended narrative. Character change. Consequence. Empathy. Big and small concepts.

title: The Day Everything Was Purple
story:
One morning, Anya woke up.
And everything was PURPLE.

The bed was purple.
The floor was purple.
Her socks were purple.

"Mumma!" she called.

Mumma came in. Mumma was purple too!

"Good morning," said purple Mumma.

They went to the kitchen.
Purple chai. Purple roti. Purple ghee.

They went outside.
The tree was purple.
The crow was purple.
The sky was purple.

Anya laughed and laughed.

"I like purple," she said. "But…"

"But what?" said Mumma.

"But where is green?
Where is the green of the leaves?

And where is blue?
Where is the blue of the sky?

And where is yellow?
Where is the yellow of my duck?"

"Hmm," said Mumma. "Shall we get them back?"

"Yes!" said Anya.

So Anya closed her eyes.
And she counted — ek, do, teen.

And she opened them.

And the leaves were GREEN.
And the sky was BLUE.
And her duck was YELLOW.

And everything was every colour again.

"That's better," said Anya.

But sometimes, just for fun,
she still likes to imagine
a purple day.
how_they_join_in: Most of a short repeating line, said along with you. Pausing just before it is what prompts them. They may also start requesting the story by its refrain rather than its title.
how_to_tell_it:
Point at real things as you name their colours in the second half. Actual leaves, actual sky.

Use the colour words heavily and repeatedly. At two this is prime colour-learning time and the story gives the words a context.

The counting with eyes closed — do it with them, eyes actually closed.

Swap purple for your child's favourite colour once they have one. The story works with any colour.

Encourage them to imagine other colour days. "What if everything was orange?" This is early imaginative thinking.
what_this_builds: Colour vocabulary. Imagination and pretend. Counting. Contrast between imagined and real.
hindi_words: chai, roti, ghee, ek do teen (one two three)

title: Pakde! The Chase Story
story:
"I am going to catch you," said Papa.

"No!" laughed Aarav. And he ran.

Papa ran after him. Slowly. Very slowly.
Big heavy steps. Thump. Thump.

"I'm coming… I'm coming…"

Aarav ran behind the sofa.
Papa looked. "Where is Aarav?"

Aarav ran under the table.
Papa looked. "Where has he gone?"

Aarav ran into the bedroom.
Papa followed. Thump. Thump.

"I'm getting closer…"

Aarav hid behind the curtain.
Only his feet were showing.

Papa said, "Hmm. I cannot see Aarav anywhere.
I suppose I will go and eat all the biscuits myself."

"NO!" shouted Aarav — and jumped out!

"GOT YOU!" said Papa.

And he picked him up and spun him round.
And Aarav laughed and laughed and laughed.

"Again!" said Aarav.

"Again?" said Papa.

"AGAIN!"
how_they_join_in: Most of a short repeating line, said along with you. Pausing just before it is what prompts them. They may also start requesting the story by its refrain rather than its title.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a story to act out, not to sit and listen to. Tell it while playing it.

Move slowly. The pleasure is entirely in the anticipation, not the catching.

"I'm coming… I'm coming…" said slowly and drawn out is the line they will beg for.

The feet showing behind the curtain — pretend not to see. Toddlers find adults being fooled hilarious.

End with "again" because they will say it. Twenty times.

This is a father-child story particularly, and worth handing to the parent who does less of the bedtime reading.
what_this_builds: Anticipation. Physical play. Hide and seek. Turn-taking. Excitement and recovery.
hindi_words: pakde (catch), names are examples — swap in your own

title: Where Does the Sun Go?
story:
"Where does the sun go at night?" asked Riya.

"Let's find out," said Nani.

So they watched.

In the morning the sun was here — low, and orange.
Good morning, sun.

At lunchtime the sun was up there — high, and bright.
Very hot!

In the evening the sun went down, down, down —
behind the buildings.
Orange again. And pink. And a bit purple.

"Bye bye, sun," said Riya.

And then it was dark.

"So where did it go?" asked Riya.

"It went to the other side," said Nani.
"To wake up other children. Far away."

"Other children?"

"Yes. And when they go to sleep,
the sun will come back here.
And wake you up."

Riya thought about that.

"So the sun is always awake?"

"Always," said Nani. "Somewhere."

Then Riya looked up.

"And the chanda? Where does chanda mama go?"

Nani laughed.
"That," she said, "is a story for tomorrow."

Goodnight, Riya.
Goodnight, sun.
Goodnight, everyone far away.
how_they_join_in: Most of a short repeating line, said along with you. Pausing just before it is what prompts them. They may also start requesting the story by its refrain rather than its title.
how_to_tell_it:
A bedtime story, told slowly.

If you can, watch an actual sunset together once and tell it then. It makes the story real.

The idea of other children far away is genuinely fascinating at two and is their first taste of a world beyond what they can see.

"That is a story for tomorrow" is a useful ending — it gives them something to look forward to and gently closes the day.

Do not over-explain the science. The story is about wonder, not astronomy.
what_this_builds: Day and night. Time concepts. Wonder and curiosity. Comfort at bedtime. Colour vocabulary.

title: The Sabzi Mandi
story:
We went to the sabzi mandi.

It was so noisy!
"Aloo! Pyaaz! Tamatar!" the vendors called.

So many colours.

Red tamatar — round and shiny.
Green mirchi — small and thin.
Orange gajar — long, with a green top.
Purple baingan — smooth and fat.
White pyaaz — with brown papery skin.

"Can I hold one?" I asked.

I held a tamatar. Smooth and cool.
I held a gajar. Bumpy and hard.
I held a bhindi. Fuzzy!

"Ooh," I said. "That one is fuzzy."

The vendor laughed. "Bhindi is always fuzzy, beta."

We put everything in the thaila.
It got heavy. Very heavy.

I helped carry it. With two hands.

And at home —

Mumma made aloo. And bhindi.
And I ate it all.

Well…
most of it.

I did not eat the mirchi.
Mirchi is too spicy for me.

Not yet.
how_they_join_in: Most of a short repeating line, said along with you. Pausing just before it is what prompts them. They may also start requesting the story by its refrain rather than its title.
how_to_tell_it:
This works best told at an actual sabzi mandi or vegetable shop, naming things as you see them.

Let them touch the vegetables. The fuzzy bhindi is the memorable one and it is genuinely surprising to a toddler.

The vendors' calls should be loud and sing-song, the way they actually are.

"Not yet" at the end acknowledges that they are small and growing, which two-year-olds like.

This story builds a vocabulary they will use daily for the rest of their life, and it makes vegetables interesting before they become a battle.
what_this_builds: Vegetable vocabulary in Hindi. Texture and colour words. Sensory exploration. Everyday outings.
hindi_words: sabzi mandi (vegetable market), aloo (potato), pyaaz (onion), tamatar (tomato), mirchi (chilli), gajar (carrot), baingan (aubergine), bhindi (okra), thaila (bag), beta

title: Guddu Cannot Sleep
story:
Guddu was in bed.
But Guddu could not sleep.

"Mumma," he called. "I need paani."

Mumma brought paani.
Guddu drank it.

"Mumma," he called. "My blanket is wrong."

Mumma fixed the blanket.

"Mumma," he called. "I heard a sound."

"That is only the fan," said Mumma.

"Mumma," he called. "I need one more story."

"You have had three stories," said Mumma.
"Now it is sleeping time."

She sat beside him.
She did not talk.
She just sat, and put her hand on his back.

Guddu lay still.

He heard the fan. Whirrr.
He heard a scooter far away. Brrmm.
He heard Mumma breathing. In. Out.

He closed one eye.
Then the other eye.

He thought about the park.
He thought about the swing.
He thought about going higher and higher and —

And Guddu was asleep.

And Mumma sat for one more minute.
And then she kissed his head,
and went quietly out.

Goodnight, Guddu.
how_they_join_in: Most of a short repeating line, said along with you. Pausing just before it is what prompts them. They may also start requesting the story by its refrain rather than its title.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a story about the bedtime stalling that is happening in your house right now, and telling it can gently reduce it.

Say each "Mumma, I need…" in the exact tone your own child uses. They find this hilarious and slightly exposing.

The turning point is when the mother stops talking and just sits. Slow right down there. Drop your voice to almost nothing.

Match the story's pace to the actual settling — by the time Guddu closes his eyes, you should be barely audible.

Do not use it as a lecture. It is a story about a child who is helped to sleep, not a child who is told off.
what_this_builds: Bedtime routine. Self-recognition. Winding down through pacing. Comfort and boundaries together.

title: The Hare and the Tortoise
story:
There was a khargosh who could run very fast.
And he knew it.

"I am the fastest!" he said. "Nobody can beat me!"

A kachua was walking by. Slowly. Very slowly.

"I will race you," said the kachua.

The khargosh laughed and laughed.
"YOU? You are so slow! Alright. Let us race."

All the animals came to watch.

"Ready… steady… GO!"

The khargosh ran. Whoosh! Away he went.
Far, far ahead.

The kachua walked. Step. Step. Step.

The khargosh looked back. He could not even see the kachua.

"I have so much time," he said.
"I will just rest under this tree."

And he lay down. And he closed his eyes.
And he fell fast asleep. Zzzzz.

And the kachua kept walking.
Step. Step. Step.

Past the tree where the khargosh was sleeping.
Step. Step. Step.

Up the hill. Step. Step. Step.
Down the hill. Step. Step. Step.

The khargosh woke up.
"Oh no! How long did I sleep?"

He ran! Fast, fast, faster than ever!

But when he got to the finish —
the kachua was already there.

All the animals were cheering.

"How?" said the khargosh. "You are so slow!"

"Yes," said the kachua. "But I did not stop.
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
Contrast is everything. The hare fast and loud; the tortoise slow and calm.

"Step. Step. Step." is theirs, and it should be genuinely slow. Slower than is comfortable. That slowness is the story.

Let them do the running with you — the hare's whoosh, arms moving fast.

Snore properly during the sleep.

Do not explain the moral. The last line does it. At two and a half they understand "he did not stop" more than they understand "slow and steady wins the race".
what_this_builds: Persistence. Contrast between characters. Extended narrative. Consequence of overconfidence.

title: The Wobbly Tooth of the Little Tiger
story:
A little baagh had a wobbly tooth.

Wobble, wobble.

"Mumma," he said. "My tooth is moving!"

"That happens," said Mumma Tiger. "A new one is coming."

"But I don't want a new one. I want THIS one."

Wobble, wobble.

He tried not to touch it.
But his tongue kept going back. Wobble.

He ate his breakfast carefully.
Wobble.

He played carefully.
Wobble, wobble.

Then he yawned — a big tiger yawn —

and the tooth fell out!

Right onto the floor. Ting!

The little baagh looked at it.
Such a small thing.

He touched the gap with his tongue.
It felt strange. Soft and empty.

"It's gone," he said. And his eyes went wet.

"I know," said Mumma. "It is a bit sad."

She sat with him.

"But look," she said. "Feel again."

He felt again.
And right at the bottom of the gap —
something hard. Something new.

A new tooth. Coming up.

"It's coming," he said.

"It's coming," said Mumma.
"Bigger and stronger than the last one."

The little baagh smiled his gappy smile.

And he kept the old tooth in a little box.
Just to remember it.
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
This is for a child who is teething or losing a tooth, and it works for both.

"Wobble, wobble" said with a wobbly voice. Let them join.

The sadness is important — do not rush past it. A two-year-old feeling sad about a change is real, and the story validates it before offering the comfort.

"Feel again" is the turn. Slow down there.

Useful for any change a child is unsettled by, not only teeth. The shape — something goes, something better comes — transfers.
what_this_builds: Emotional processing of change. Body awareness. Validation before reassurance. Growth as a positive.

title: The Day Dadi Came
story:
On Friday, Mumma said: "Dadi is coming tomorrow."

"Tomorrow?" said Ishaan.

"Tomorrow. After you sleep, and wake up, and eat breakfast."

Ishaan waited.

He waited while he had his bath.
He waited while he ate his dinner.
He waited while he brushed his teeth.

"Is it tomorrow?"

"Not yet. First you sleep."

So he slept.

And in the morning — he woke up and ran to Mumma.

"IS IT TOMORROW?"

"It is TODAY," said Mumma. "Dadi comes today."

They cleaned the house.
They made Dadi's bed.
Ishaan put one toy on the pillow. For Dadi.

Then — the doorbell.

Ding dong!

Ishaan ran to the door.

And there was Dadi!
With her bag, and her smell of coconut oil,
and her big soft arms.

"Ishaan!" she said. "You have grown so big!"

She had brought laddoo.
She had brought a story.
And she had brought her lap,
which was the best thing of all.

That night, Dadi told him a story about when Papa was small.

"Papa was small?" said Ishaan.

"Very small," said Dadi. "Smaller than you."

Ishaan thought that was the funniest thing he had ever heard.
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
Change Dadi to whoever actually visits — Nani, Bua, Chachu, Mausi.

"Is it tomorrow?" is theirs, and it will get real laughs because it is exactly what they do.

Slow down on the arrival. The smell of coconut oil, the soft arms — these sensory details are what make a grandparent real in a story.

"Papa was small?" is the joke and it genuinely delights a two-year-old. The idea that adults were once children is new information at this age.

Tell it before a real visit. It builds anticipation and helps with the waiting.
what_this_builds: Time concepts (tomorrow, today). Anticipation and waiting. Family relationships. Generational time.

title: Bandar Bandar, What Do You See?
story:
Bandar, bandar, what do you see?

I see a hathi looking at me.

Hathi, hathi, what do you see?

I see a sher looking at me.

Sher, sher, what do you see?

I see a mor looking at me.

Mor, mor, what do you see?

I see a saanp looking at me.

Saanp, saanp, what do you see?

I see a chidiya looking at me.

Chidiya, chidiya, what do you see?

I see a bacha looking at me.

Bacha, bacha, what do you see?

I see…

a bandar,
a hathi,
a sher,
a mor,
a saanp,
and a chidiya —

all looking at me!

And I look back at all of them.

Hello, everyone!
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a chant more than a story. Get a rhythm going and keep it.

Each animal gets a voice and, if you can, a hand shape or gesture. The peacock's fanned tail, the snake's hand.

The final list should build in speed and volume. Then stop dead on "all looking at me!"

By twenty-six months many children can supply the next animal. Pause and let them.

Once they know it, let them choose the animals and build a new version. That is where it becomes theirs.
what_this_builds: Animal vocabulary. Repetitive predictable structure. Memory and sequence. Participation.
hindi_words: bandar (monkey), hathi (elephant), sher (lion), mor (peacock), saanp (snake), chidiya (bird), bacha (child)

title: The Broken Cup
story:
Meera was carrying her cup.
Her favourite cup. The yellow one with the duck.

She was walking carefully.
Very carefully.

But then she saw the cat.
And she looked at the cat.
And she did not look at her feet.

And —

CRASH.

The cup fell.
And it broke into three pieces.

Meera stood very still.

Her tummy felt strange. Tight.

Mumma came in.

Meera looked at the floor.
"I broke it," she said. Very quietly.

Mumma looked at the pieces.
Then she looked at Meera.

"Thank you for telling me," she said.

"Are you angry?"

"I am a little bit sad about the cup," said Mumma.
"But cups break. That happens.
And I am glad you told me straight away."

They cleaned it up together.
Careful with the sharp bits.

"Can we fix it?" asked Meera.

"Not this one," said Mumma. "It is too broken."

Meera's eyes went wet.

"It's alright to be sad," said Mumma. "It was your favourite."

So they sat together for a minute.

And then they found another cup.
A blue one. With a fish.

"This one can be my favourite now," said Meera.

"It can," said Mumma. "And guess what?
You are still my favourite, always,
even when things break."
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
This story does a lot of quiet work. It is about honesty being safe.

Say "thank you for telling me" warmly and clearly. That is the sentence you want them to remember, and it will matter enormously at fourteen.

Do not skip the sadness or fix it too fast. The pause where they sit together is the most important part.

Tell it at a calm time, not immediately after your child has broken something. Then it is a story, not a lesson.

The final line should be said looking right at them.
what_this_builds: Honesty and safety. Emotional processing. Accidents versus wrongdoing. Repair and unconditional love.

title: Titli, Titli — The Butterfly
story:
On a leaf there was a tiny egg.
So small you could hardly see it.

Then out came a caterpillar.
A small, hungry caterpillar.

He ate one leaf. Munch.
He ate two leaves. Munch, munch.
He ate three leaves. Munch, munch, munch!

He grew.
And he grew.
And he GREW.

Then he was tired. So tired.

So he made a little house around himself.
A quiet brown house, hanging from a branch.

And he went to sleep.

Days went by.
The wind blew. The rain came.
The little house stayed quiet.

Then — one morning —
something moved.

Crack.

A small hole appeared.

And out came…

first one wing.
Then the other wing.

Orange and black and beautiful.

A titli!

She opened her wings. Slowly.
She dried them in the dhoop.

And then —

she flew.

Up, up, over the tree.
Over the wall.
Over the whole garden.

The little caterpillar who could only crawl
was now a titli who could fly.
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
The munching is theirs. Big chewing sounds.

"He grew. And he grew. And he GREW." — get bigger and slower each time, and stretch out your arms.

Go completely quiet for the cocoon part. Whisper the days going by.

"Crack" should be small and sudden.

The flying at the end — stand up if you can, and let them fly around the room.

If you can find an actual caterpillar or butterfly to look at afterwards, this story becomes ten times more powerful.
what_this_builds: Life cycle and change. Patience and transformation. Growth vocabulary. Wonder at the natural world.

title: Two Friends and One Ladoo
story:
Anu and Vir found one ladoo.
Just one.

"I want it," said Anu.
"I want it," said Vir.

They both held it.
They both pulled.

"Mine!"
"MINE!"

And the ladoo fell on the floor.
And a crow came down — kaa! — and took it away.

Anu and Vir looked at each other.

No ladoo for anybody.

They sat down. They were both cross.
And a bit sad.

Then Anu's Nani came out.
She had a plate.
And on the plate — two more ladoo.

"One for you," she said. "And one for you."

Anu took hers.
Vir took his.

They sat on the step and ate them.
Crumbs everywhere.

"That was better," said Vir.

"Yes," said Anu. "Next time — we can break it in half."

"Half for you," said Vir.
"And half for me," said Anu.

And the crow sat on the wall,
hoping they would drop another one.
how_they_join_in: The full repeating line, unprompted, once they know the story. They will also begin objecting if you change any word — which is a sign the story has been properly learned.
how_to_tell_it:
The tug of war should be physical. Do it with a cushion or a toy, both of you pulling.

The crow taking it is the moment they gasp. Make it sudden.

Do not moralise. The children work it out themselves in the story, which is the point.

"Break it in half" is a concept a two-and-a-half-year-old can genuinely use. Demonstrate it with a real biscuit afterwards.

The crow at the end waiting for another one is the joke.
what_this_builds: Sharing. Natural consequence. Problem-solving. Friendship repair. Fairness.

title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
story:
On the riverbank there was a jamun tree.
And in the tree lived a bandar.

The jamun were sweet and purple and delicious.

One day a magarmach came to the river.
He was hungry and tired.

"Would you like some jamun?" called the bandar.
And he threw some down.

The magarmach ate them. "Delicious!" he said.

Every day after that, the bandar gave him jamun.
And they became friends.

One day the magarmach said,
"My wife would love these jamun too."

So the bandar sent some home with him.

But the magarmach's wife was not a kind crocodile.
"If the monkey eats such sweet fruit every day,"
she said, "his heart must be the sweetest of all.
Bring me the monkey's heart."

The magarmach was very sad.
But he did what his wife said.

"Friend," he called. "Come to my house for dinner!
Sit on my back. I will carry you across the river."

The bandar was happy. He climbed on.

They swam. Out into the middle of the river.

Then the magarmach said, "I must tell you something.
My wife wants to eat your heart."

The bandar was frightened!
But he thought fast. Very fast.

"Oh no!" he said. "Why didn't you tell me before?
I don't keep my heart with me.
I leave it hanging in the jamun tree!"

"Really?" said the magarmach.

"Yes! Take me back and I will get it."

So the magarmach swam back to the bank.

And the bandar jumped —
up, up, into the tree!

He sat on a high branch and looked down.

"Silly friend," he said. "Nobody leaves their heart in a tree.
And nobody stays friends with someone who wants to eat them."

And the magarmach swam away, alone.

And the bandar ate his jamun in peace.
repeating_line: Sit on my back. I will carry you across the river.
how_they_join_in: The line, and often a few words of what comes next. Try stopping mid-sentence anywhere in the story and letting them finish it. Many can.
how_to_tell_it:
This is a longer story and a two-and-a-half-year-old can follow it. Take your time.

The friendship at the start needs to feel warm so the betrayal lands.

The frightening part should be brief and immediately followed by the monkey's cleverness. Do not linger in the fear.

"I leave it hanging in the jamun tree" — say it with cheeky confidence. This is the moment children love.

The lesson at the end is about who deserves friendship, which is a genuinely useful idea to plant early. Say it plainly and move on.
what_this_builds: Extended narrative with a twist. Quick thinking. Friendship and trust. Classic tale exposure.

title: The Big Feeling
story:
Ved wanted the blue cup.
Mumma gave him the green cup.

And something happened inside Ved.

It started in his tummy.
A hot, tight feeling.

It went up to his chest.
It went up to his face.

And it came out —

"NOOOOO!"

He threw the green cup.
He lay on the floor.
He kicked his legs.

The feeling was SO BIG.
Bigger than Ved.

Mumma sat down on the floor near him.
She did not shout.
She did not go away.

She just sat.

Ved cried and cried.

And then — slowly —
the big feeling started to get smaller.

His legs stopped kicking.
His crying got quieter.
His breathing got slower.

Mumma opened her arms.

And Ved crawled into them.

She held him tight.

"That was a very big feeling," she said.

"Big," said Ved.

"You wanted the blue cup."

"Blue cup," said Ved. And his eyes went wet again.

"I know," said Mumma. "The blue cup is in the wash.
It will be clean tomorrow."

They sat together for a while.

Then Ved got up.
And he drank his milk from the green cup.

And the big feeling was gone.

Until next time.
Because big feelings come back.
And that's alright.
Mumma will always sit down on the floor.
repeating_line: That was a very big feeling.
how_they_join_in: The line, and often a few words of what comes next. Try stopping mid-sentence anywhere in the story and letting them finish it. Many can.
how_to_tell_it:
Tell this at a calm time, never during or immediately after a tantrum.

The description of the feeling rising through the body is the useful part. It gives them language for something they experience physically and cannot name.

The mother doing nothing except staying is the whole model. Do not add anything to it.

"Until next time. Because big feelings come back." — this normalises it rather than promising it will stop, which would not be true.

Many children ask for this story repeatedly. That is a sign it is doing something.
